content.theory:
A C-style **array** holds a fixed number of same-typed values:

```cpp
int scores[4];                    // 4 ints, uninitialized
int nums[] = {10, 20, 30};        // sized from initializer
```

Access by index — 0-based:

```cpp
scores[0] = 95;
std::cout << nums[1] << std::endl;   // 20
std::cout << nums[2] << std::endl;   // 30
```

**Vectors** (from `<vector>`) are the modern growable alternative:

```cpp
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> v = {10, 20, 30};
v.push_back(40);          // add to end → {10,20,30,40}
v.size()                  // 4
v[0]                      // 10
v.pop_back();             // remove last
```

Loop over arrays and vectors the same way:

```cpp
for (int n : nums) {
    std::cout << n << std::endl;
}
```

Key differences:

| | Array | Vector |
|--|-------|--------|
| Size | fixed | growable |
| Header | — | `<vector>` |
| Methods | none | push_back, size, pop_back |

The classic C++ array bug: accessing `nums[5]` when the array has 3 items — no error, just garbage data or a crash.

exercise.instruction: Write the program: include <vector>, create std::vector<int> 'v' with {1, 2, 3}, push_back(4), then use a range-based for loop to print each value.
hints: Hint 3: for (int n : v) std::cout << n << std::endl;
